taking down from the crofs from Rubens.<x_0.7568><y_0.0352><class_Text>

<x_0.0234><y_0.0281>There is a fine influence of linear effect in a print of
a Flemish conversation piece by Wille. One of the
figures is drinking out of a glafs, and the artif has molt
deceptively described the texture of the drinker's face
through the glafs. In the fame print, a female figure
fhews great kill in this way, even the floor is charac-
terized by lines; and the whole strongly marks the molt
proper mode of treating subjects of a mere local nature.
The beautiful print of the _Petit Phufcien_, is alfo an ad-
mirable imitation, particularly the little pellucid globule
which has jult mounted from the flell. When lines are
engraved in a square acute method of crolling, they ge-
nerally convey the idea of hardness to the fuljed repre-
fented. The scientific Picart feems to have been fo much
aware of this, that in a print of his engraving of a large
marble groupe of horses, from the animated chiffel of
Perriere, he adopted this flyle in order to heighten the
imitation.<x_0.7578><y_0.3289><class_Text>

<x_0.0186><y_0.3219>Maison’s print of Marthal Harcourt, is one of the many
fine efforts of portrait engraving ; and although it was
executed at an early period of the art, it abounds with
no final degree of tafte. The celebrated print (called
the table-cloth) from Titian, of the Laft Supper, allo
contains a considerable degree of linear discrimination,
although he sometimes carries it to affectation. He is
rather singular in his mode of engraving hair. Yet the
portraits of Marthal Harcourt and Brilafiere the ferre-
tary may be deemed exceptions.<x_0.749><y_0.4945><class_Text>

<x_0.0127><y_0.4852>Wille, by the magic of his tooling, is too apt at times
to give his works indirferinately the appearance of
bronze ; and we frequently find the fame in the figures
of Balechow: but it feems to have been referred for
Strange to give the foltnels of carnation to copper ; and
to Woollet, to give force and clearnels with diferimi-
nating tafte. Bartolozzi in his lines elegance delicacy
and drawing ; while the works of Audran team with
boldnefs and implicity. In the prints of Sir Robert
Strange, the greatest excellence is perhaps his rich and
harmonious tones, as well as the whole effect, which is
fupported by an exprelive flyle ; which he feems in a
great mesure to have invented for his most favourite
painters, Corregio, Titian, Guido, and Guerchino. The
foltnels, the gullo, and the flowing draperies in the
works of these matters, were his delight. His sleeping
Cupid from Guido, and the prints of the Venus and
Danae from Titian, will ever be efteemed as _chef_
d'avures in the linear art.<x_0.75><y_0.8039><class_Text>

<x_0.0078><y_0.7953>Having thus attempted to fulfil our original intention
of discriminating the molt exprellive combinations of
lines, and of analyzing and illustrating their various
powers and effects in engraving, we shall now conclude
these observations; and if, from the nature of the fub-
ject, and from the limits of the sketch, we have failed
in marking every brilliant flat in the galaxy of the art ;
it mult at leaft be acknowledged, that we have not
omitted some of those of the fruit magnitude.<x_0.7373><y_0.9539><class_Text>

<x_0.0391><y_0.9453>_ENGRAFINA upon Glafr._ See GLASS, Engraving on.
_ENGRAVING_<x_0.7236><y_0.9867><class_Caption>
